scenes.name: Funk industrial
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras la caída de P-Funk, muchos ritmos nuevos vinieron de fuera: Kraftwerk, Art of Noise («Beat Box», «Close (to the Edit)»), Talking Heads (Stop Making Sense, con Bernie Worrell) y el «Genius of Love» de Tom Tom Club. Herbie Hancock pidió a su mánager Tony Meilandt unos temas de hip hop y con Bill Laswell y Grandmixer D.S.T. hizo «Rockit» (Future Shock, 1983): la cima del funk industrial nada más empezar. Laswell (Material, Time Zone con John Lydon, Manu Dibango, los Last Poets) dejó su sello de bajo grueso; sellos como Celluloid, On-U Sound, Tommy Boy o Def Jam sacaban ritmos ásperos de raspados metálicos y tensión de Guerra Fría. On-U Sound de Adrian Sherwood fichó a la sección rítmica de Sugarhill (Doug Wimbish, Skip McDonald, Keith LeBlanc): Tackhead, el «No Sell Out» con la voz de Malcolm X, «el P-Funk de los ochenta» según Pedro Bell.
scenes.family: Hip hop, go-go y funk de los noventa

scenes.name: On-U Sound y el dub blanco
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Adrian Sherwood, fanático blanco del reggae que vendía discos desde su camioneta y aprendió solo a ser ingeniero, forma New Age Steppers con Ari Up y los Creation Rebel («Fade Away», 1981). Mark Stewart debuta en solitario con Sherwood: su «Jerusalem» (1982) une la Albión de Blake con el Sión rasta entre órgano de iglesia y bajos de dub.
scenes.family: Vanguardia postpunk: dub, funk y política

scenes.name: Post-punk dub (On-U Sound)
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: El punk, el funk y el dub se entretejen: el estudio como instrumento. The Slits con Dennis Bovell, The Pop Group en Bristol y, sobre todo, Adrian Sherwood y su sello On-U Sound: New Age Steppers, African Head Charge (precursor del techno-dub) y Tackhead, banda de estudio que endureció el sonido hacia el funk industrial y politizado.

podcast.title: Producer for Ministry's "Twitch" (1986)
podcast.body: In 1986, Al Jourgensen collaborated with Adrian Sherwood to produce the album "Twitch." Jourgensen was drawn to Sherwood's signature style of heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops. "He jumped at the chance to work with Adrian. And the result was the 1986 album entitled Twitch."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Radical Remixes for Depeche Mode
podcast.body: Adrian Sherwood created "pretty radical remixes" for Depeche Mode songs like "People Are People" and "Master and Servant," characterized by heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops. These remixes were highly influential, particularly on Al Jourgensen of Ministry. "Adrian had created some pretty radical remixes for Depeche Mode, most notably for people are people and master and servant."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with Adrian Sherwood (1986)
xref.body: In 1986, through connections related to Depeche Mode, Jourgensen partnered with producer Adrian Sherwood, whose radical remixing style, emphasizing heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops, greatly influenced Jourgensen and led to the album "Twitch." "But in 1986, through some Depeche Mode connections, he hooked up with producer Adrian Sherwood."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transition to Industrial Sound (1986)
xref.body: After being dropped by his record label and dabbling in goth music (1984-1985), Al Jourgensen restarted his career. In 1986, through Depeche Mode connections, he collaborated with producer Adrian Sherwood. Sherwood's radical remixes (e.g., for Depeche Mode) impressed Jourgensen with their heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops, leading to the industrial-leaning album "Twitch." "But in 1986, through some Depeche Mode connections, he hooked up with producer Adrian Sherwood."

xref.title: Toured with Ministry's early band
xref.body: Depeche Mode toured with Alan Jourgensen's early Technopop band from Chicago, providing an important connection that would later see Jourgensen work with Adrian Sherwood, who also remixed Depeche Mode tracks. "Alan was in a Tectopop band from Chicago that had spent some time touring with both Depeche Mode and Culture Club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
